extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, publishers, and scholarly-communication stakeholders interested in peer review innovation
extracted.subtask_description: A conceptual framework describing four ‘‘schools of thought’’ that characterize different priorities and evaluative criteria for improving peer review in scholarly publishing. The paper surveys innovations, evidence, examples, and tensions between perspectives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality & Reproducibility school
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on the role peer review can play in ensuring published research is of a high quality and, wherever possible, reproducible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasizes improving the quality of review reports (e.g., reviewer training, use of checklists, statistical reviewers, revealing reviewer identities, anonymizing authors). Concerned with inter-rater reliability, reproducibility (e.g., registered reports), peer review of data and software, and detection/safeguarding of research integrity. Cites systematic reviews (Bruce et al., Bornmann) that highlight limited or mixed empirical evidence and call for more experimentation and evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inter-rater reliability (agreement between reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of agreement between different peer reviewers of the same manuscript as an indicator of reliability of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Low inter-rater reliability has been widely reported and seen by some as problematic (suggesting a 'game of chance'), leading to proposals for more reviewers per manuscript; others argue low agreement can be acceptable because reviewers bring different expertise. Evidence summarized by Bornmann and Bornmann et al.; implications include reconsidering reviewer selection, diversity, and number of reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Registered reports (peer review before data collection)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review of a research plan and in-principle acceptance before carrying out data collection and analysis to improve quality and reproducibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registered reports aim to reduce biases (preference for positive, novel, or unequivocal results) and are associated with reviewers perceiving greater rigour and quality without reducing importance or creativity. Papers still require later peer review for analyses and inferences that cannot be pre-assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review of research inputs (data and software)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadening peer review beyond papers to include datasets and software underlying research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: PLOS 'five quick checks' for data peer review; Mayernik et al.'s four scenarios for data peer review; CODECHECK for computational workflow checking. Emphasizes that data/software review is not monolithic and that different modes (data papers, repository checks, journal-linked datasets) exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research integrity detection and use of forensic tools
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of software and publisher workflows to detect plagiarism, image manipulation, poor statistical analyses, and organized fraud (paper mills).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text similarity scanners are now widely adopted; other tools detect image manipulation and statistical anomalies. Publishers coordinate via initiatives like the STM Integrity Hub and may retract batches of suspicious papers. Recognizes limits: reviewers often cannot detect deliberate fabrication, but tools increase detectability of some misconduct forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy & Transparency school
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on making the evaluation of scientific research more open, accountable and democratic by broadening participation and increasing transparency of peer-review processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates opening participation to broader groups, publishing reviewer reports, decision letters and author responses, and (in some variants) publishing reviewer identities. Also includes models that shift gatekeeping (soundness-only review, publish-then-review) and platforms enabling community-led post-publication evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Soundness-only peer review (mega-journal model)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluative model that accepts manuscripts based only on methodological soundness and rigour, leaving judgments about novelty, significance and relevance to the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practiced by mega-journals like PLOS ONE and Scientific Reports; intended to democratize evaluation by moving from editorial selection to community appraisal. Motivations include resisting elitism and gatekeeping, though this assumes a capable community to judge significance post-publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparent/open peer review (publishing reports and/or reviewer identities)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing peer review reports, editor decision letters, and sometimes reviewer names alongside the article to increase accountability and reusability of review content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pioneered by BMJ, BMC, EMBO; argued to be ethically superior to anonymous review and to increase reviewer accountability. Evidence includes trials (e.g., Van Rooyen et al.) and growing journal adoption; may also contribute to quality improvements by increasing scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish-then-review and post-publication peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Models that invert traditional pre-publication gatekeeping by publishing manuscripts (often as preprints) and conducting open or community review afterwards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: F1000Research (immediate publication + open soundness-only review), eLife's 'publish, then review' and 'Reviewed Preprint' model, platforms like ScienceOpen, Peer Community In, PREreview, and Publish Your Reviews initiative. Framed as 'publish then filter' or 'publish, then curate' approaches to increase transparency and community engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equity & Inclusion school
rubrics_metrics.description: Emphasis on diversity, inclusion, and equity within peer review to ensure balanced representation of demographic and geographic groups among gatekeepers (editors, reviewers) and influence which knowledge gets produced and disseminated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Calls for active recruitment of diverse editorial boards and reviewers (COPE recommendations), publisher commitments (Joint commitment for action on inclusion and diversity), collecting diversity data (gender, race/ethnicity), and policy changes to reduce bias (e.g., double-anonymous review). Links lack of diversity to gaps in 'knowledge by acquaintance.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Double-anonymous (double-blind) peer review to reduce bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Concealing both reviewer and author identities to reduce bias related to gender, geography, reputation, or institutional affiliation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: IOP Publishing's move to universal double-anonymous review cited as an example; social sciences and humanities have longer traditions of double-anonymous review. Evidence for effectiveness is mixed; status bias literature (e.g., Huber et al.) motivates adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence standards for claims of bias in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: The need for robust empirical evidence (experimental designs rather than observational) before concluding that peer review is biased by author characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most studies are observational and may not control for confounders or manuscript quality; experimental studies report no evidence of bias. Authors call for more rigorous research covering gender, geography, ethnicity, and status, and for multiple theoretical perspectives (beyond positivist) to understand equity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency & Incentives school
rubrics_metrics.description: Focus on streamlining peer review processes to reduce delays and reviewer burden, and on incentivizing participation through recognition, credit or payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses reviewer fatigue and imbalance whereby a minority do most reviews. Innovations include portable peer review, journal-independent review, recognition platforms, and proposals to pay reviewers. Evaluations of cost/feasibility and incentive effects are part of this school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portable peer review and cascading reuse of reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Reuse of review reports when manuscripts move between journals to avoid repeated reviewing and speed publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practiced within publisher portfolios (cascading) and via cross-publisher initiatives (Neuroscience Peer Review Consortium). Manuscript Exchange Common Approach (MECA) supports technical interoperability. Aims to reduce wasted reviewer time and publication delays, though cultural and technical challenges remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journal-independent peer review (e.g., Review Commons)
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review conducted independently of journals (often on preprints) with reviews transferable to journals, allowing assessment of study quality rather than fit to a journal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review Commons provides journal-independent review for life-sciences preprints; authors can then submit revised manuscripts and reviews to participating journals. Intended to accelerate communication and reduce repeated review cycles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognition and credit mechanisms for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Giving visibility and formal recognition to peer review activities to incentivize reviewers (e.g., Publons, ORCID integrations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publons (now integrated into Clarivate/Web of Science) and ORCID allow reviewers to record and showcase reviewing. Aim is to speed science by improving reward structures rather than increasing workload; recognition can be public acknowledgement or verified records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paying peer reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing direct monetary compensation to peer reviewers as a form of recognition and incentive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocates argue payment could accelerate reviews and improve quality; skeptics point to high suggested per-review rates (e.g., $450) and limited funds in the system to sustain broad payment policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addressing reviewer fatigue and distribution of reviewing burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Reducing burden on an overworked minority of reviewers and expanding the reviewer pool to make peer review sustainable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strategies include incentives (recognition, payment), efficiency measures (portable/journal-independent review), reviewer training to broaden capacity, and technology-assisted triage. The paper highlights estimates of millions of papers and millions of reviewer-hours per year to motivate this concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training and structured review templates/checklists
rubrics_metrics.description: Interventions aimed at improving the quality of review reports via training and standardized templates/checklists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systematic reviews (Bruce et al.) cast doubt on the effectiveness of training and templates for improving article quality or review quality; evidence is limited and further experimentation is called for. Checklists are nonetheless commonly proposed as a quality-improvement tool.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical and specialist peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Engaging specialist statistical reviewers or other domain experts to improve methodological assessment and paper quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meta-analyses find statistical peer review can improve paper quality; adding specialist reviewers is highlighted as a practical innovation within the Quality & Reproducibility school.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publishing review-related artifacts alongside articles
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishing not only reviews but also editorial decision letters and authors' response letters to enhance transparency and reuse of review content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EMBO and other publishers argue review reports are valuable published analyses; publishing the full review package can make reviewer insights available and helpful for readers, editors, and future reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprint peer review integration and platforms for preprint review
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizing robust peer review around preprints to capture community feedback and formal evaluation outside traditional journal processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platforms like PREreview, Peer Community In and others enable peer review of preprints, sometimes with the explicit goal of making review more equitable and inclusive. Preprint review can serve both quality-improvement and democratic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognizing complementarities and tensions between improvement goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding that aims (quality, democracy, equity, efficiency) can be complementary but also in tension, requiring trade-offs or integrated solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper argues organizations may embrace multiple schools but must negotiate potential incompatibilities (e.g., openness vs. anonymity; efficiency vs. inclusive deliberation). It recommends using the four-school framework to facilitate conversations across stakeholders with differing priorities.
